title: Inference and Margin of Error, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with inference and margins of error, and then a reading checklist that makes these questions fast.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. A confidence interval is about a population parameter, such as a mean or a percent. Students read it as a statement about individual members.
The interval describes the population mean. It says the mean nightly sleep is plausibly between six point eight and seven point four hours, not that most students fall in that range.
beats.right: the mean is plausibly 6.8 to 7.4 hours

beats.say: Trap two. A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error, but it does not remove bias. A survey of five thousand volunteers can still misrepresent the population.
Random selection is what makes a sample representative. A large sample that was not chosen at random can still be biased.
Trap three. A sample of seniors at one school only tells you about seniors at that school. Students extend the result to everyone.
beats.wrong: seniors at one school: all students

beats.say: A conclusion can only be extended to the population the sample was randomly chosen from. Here, that is the seniors at that school.
beats.right: applies to seniors at that school

beats.say: Trap four. If the question asks how many phones are not defective, the estimate of five hundred forty is the wrong group.
Subtract from the total. Fifteen thousand minus five hundred forty is fourteen thousand four hundred sixty phones that are not defective.
Trap five. The margin of error is half the width of the interval. Students use the full width, and get twice the correct margin.
Divide the width by two. Five point six divided by two is two point eight, which is the margin of error.

Desmos adds little here, because the math is one multiplication or one midpoint. The fast way is a reading habit. For estimates, find the sample fraction, then multiply by the population, and simplify first when you can.
For intervals, convert everything to the form from L to U, and compare the endpoints directly. For sampling questions, ask whether the sample was chosen at random, and from which group.
For conclusions, eliminate any choice that says proves, all, or exactly, and any choice that talks about individuals instead of the population mean or percent.
Use Desmos only as a calculator for awkward numbers. Nine over two hundred fifty of fifteen thousand can be typed in one line, so that nothing is rounded too early.
Open a fresh graph. We type the sample fraction and then multiply by the shipment size.
Type nine, a slash, and two hundred fifty, then press the right arrow to leave the fraction. Then type times fifteen thousand.
Desmos shows five hundred forty, matching our earlier estimate of the defective phones.

Now a practice problem. A random sample of eighty bulbs from a batch of four thousand has three defective bulbs. Estimate the number of defective bulbs in the batch. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.

card.sub: Batch of 4,000. Estimate the defective count.

beats.say: Simplify first. Four thousand divided by eighty is fifty, so the fraction of the batch becomes three times fifty.
Four thousand divided by eighty is fifty. So the expression becomes three times fifty.
Three times fifty is one hundred fifty. So we estimate about one hundred fifty defective bulbs in the batch.
Check that the sample proportion matches. One hundred fifty out of four thousand is three out of eighty, which is the sample proportion.
To recap. Intervals describe a population parameter, not individuals. A bigger sample does not fix a biased sample.
beats.item: Parameters, not individuals; size is not bias

beats.say: Conclusions apply only to the sampled population. The margin of error is half the width, and use the complement when asked for not.
Use the reading checklist for every question. In the next topic, we study how to evaluate statistical claims.
